demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
**Vignette: Marivic**

Marivic is a sixty-year-old Filipino woman who has been married for thirty-four years and works the overnight shift at a call center in Manila, handling customer complaints for an international telecommunications company. She is soft-spoken and precise in the way she chooses her words, a habit she attributes to decades of training herself to stay calm on the phone no matter what is happening on the other end of the line.

Fourteen months ago, her youngest son, Rodel, died suddenly of a cardiac arrest at thirty-one years old. He had complained of fatigue for a few days, nothing that alarmed anyone. He was young and strong. On a Tuesday morning, while Marivic was sleeping after her night shift, her husband found Rodel unresponsive on the bathroom floor. By the time she was shaken awake and ran down the hallway, the paramedics were already there. She remembers standing in the doorway in her house slippers, watching them work on her son, and thinking that she needed to move but her legs had simply stopped belonging to her.

Rodel was pronounced dead at the hospital. No one had seen it coming. There was no illness to prepare for, no goodbye. He was there, and then he was not.

In the weeks that followed, Marivic returned to work because she did not know what else to do with the hours. Her husband grieved openly — he wept, he talked to relatives, he visited the grave every Sunday. Marivic did none of these things, at least not in any way that felt real to her. She moved through the house and through her shifts as though she were operating herself from a slight distance, watching herself pour coffee, watching herself put on her headset, watching herself say *thank you for calling* in a voice that sounded like hers but felt borrowed.

She no longer sleeps well. She wakes in the early afternoon — her schedule reversed by years of night work — and lies in the dark replaying the image of the paramedics in the hallway. She does not dream of Rodel as he was when he was alive, laughing or eating or watching television beside her. She dreams of the bathroom doorway, the sound of equipment, the particular quality of light that morning. Some days she wakes with her heart hammering and has to sit at the edge of the bed for several minutes before she can convince herself that the day is ordinary.

At work, she is still considered one of the best agents on the floor — patient, articulate, almost impossible to rattle. But when a caller becomes distressed, or when someone on the line begins to cry, something tightens in her chest that she cannot easily release. Twice she has had to mute her headset and press her hand flat against her sternum until the feeling passed. Her supervisor has noticed that she takes longer breaks now and has asked if she is alright. Marivic always says yes.

She has not been able to go into the bathroom on the ground floor of her home. She uses the one upstairs. Her husband has not asked about this. She is grateful he has not asked.

What troubles her most, she says, is not the grief itself — she knows she is supposed to grieve — but the way she feels sealed off from it, as though the loss is pressed against thick glass. She cannot cry at the grave the way her husband does. She feels guilty for this, and guilty for still being alive and eating breakfast and answering phone calls while Rodel is gone. She wonders sometimes, during the long quiet hours of her shift when the call queue is empty, whether she missed something, whether there was a sign she should have seen, whether a different version of that Tuesday morning exists somewhere in which she was already awake when it happened.

She has not yet found an answer that satisfies her. She keeps answering the phone.
